rationale: B wins because it gives the founder three usable lanes: DTC reversal, Sephora distribution scale, and fragrance category. A has one strong blade in "Glossier says wholesale is now its fastest-growing channel," but it dulls it with the invented flourish "after a decade of treating retail as the enemy" and then spends a second angle on the same DTC obituary. B's "A brand born from a beauty blog is now betting on the perfume aisle" is conditional, but at least it recognizes the fragrance launch as a real separate story instead of throwing it in the trash.
gaps_in_A: "after a decade of treating retail as the enemy" is not in the facts. DTC-only is not the same as anti-retail; that line needs evidence or it gets cut.
The first two angles are too close: "DTC-vs.-wholesale debate" and "verdict... for the narrative" are different temperatures of the same soup.
"the one who never made it to the prestige mall" invents a shopper and geography claim from the mere presence of Sephora at Kohl's.

Refusing "Glossier launches three-product fragrance line alongside Sephora expansion" is too absolute. The fact block says this is the first fragrance line extension; weak on details, yes, but not automatically dead.
gaps_in_B: "quietly became a wholesale company" overstates the facts. Fastest-growing channel does not mean majority channel, revenue engine, or company identity.
"collapse of the direct-to-consumer thesis" is loaded beyond the update. It can be a reported question, not a declared fact.
"Glossier was a poster child for DTC-only branding" relies on outside knowledge not supplied in the update. True enough to many beauty reporters, but this brief asked for grounded angles.
The fragrance angle needs product detail fast. "betting on the perfume aisle" works only if the three products have positioning, price, or retail-fit evidence behind them.
